reading.title: A repair café in town
reading.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
reading.passage:
When a toaster stopped working, I nearly put it in the bin. Then my neighbour told me about the repair café at the community centre. It opens one Saturday a month, and volunteers help visitors repair small household objects. I was unsure whether I could fix anything, but the volunteer showed me how to test the cable safely. The toaster worked again after ten minutes.

The café is not a shop, and the volunteers do not promise that every object can be repaired. People bring old lamps, toys and clothes, and they learn by watching or helping. Last month, a retired electrician taught two teenagers how to replace a plug. They came back this week with a radio they had repaired at home.

My favourite part is the friendly atmosphere. Visitors can have tea while they wait, and someone usually brings a cake. The project also has a practical benefit: fewer things are thrown away. The organisers hope to open on two Saturdays each month, but they need more volunteers before they can do that.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer visit the repair café?
options: The writer wanted to repair a toaster.
The community centre was selling kitchen equipment.

options: Explained how to test the cable safely.
Replaced the toaster with another one.
Asked the writer to buy a new tool.

options: They returned after repairing a radio themselves.
They opened a repair café at home.

reading.title: A new cycle route
reading.instructions: Five sentences have been removed from the text. Choose the correct sentence for each gap. There is one extra sentence.
reading.passage: Last year, the town council asked residents how to make short journeys easier. [1] Many people said they would cycle if they felt safer near the busy shopping street. [2] The council painted a cycle lane and added signs at both ends. Work began in March, just before the weather became warmer. [3] During the first week, volunteers stood nearby and explained how to use the new route. They also asked cyclists to report any problems. [4] One corner was difficult to see, so the council moved a small sign. Since then, more parents have used the route to take their children to school. [5] The council now plans to connect it to the railway station.

In response, they planned a route away from the main road.
Local cyclists were invited to test the lane when it opened.

listening.title: A town clean-up day
listening.instructions: Listen and complete the notes with one word in each gap.
listening.script: Hello, everyone. I am Priya, and I am organising our town clean-up day. We will meet at the library at nine o’clock on Saturday. Please wear old clothes because we will paint the wooden benches as well as collect litter. The council will provide bags and brushes. We will work in the park until one o’clock, then have lunch together. Bring a bottle of water, but sandwiches will be provided by the café. If you need to borrow gloves, tell me when you arrive.

listening.title: An interview with a town planner
listening.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.
listening.script: Interviewer: Alex, why did you become a town planner? Alex: I studied geography at college. During a work placement, I helped improve a small square near a school. People used it more after we added seats and trees, and I wanted to do similar work. Interviewer: What is your current project? Alex: We are planning a safer route for people walking to the hospital. The main challenge is the busy morning traffic. Interviewer: How do you know what local people need? Alex: We organise meetings and ask residents to complete surveys. We also speak with shop owners because they understand how the area changes during the day. Interviewer: What part of your work do you enjoy? Alex: Seeing people use a place that we have improved. Even a small change can make a daily journey easier. Interviewer: What advice would you give someone interested in this job? Alex: Learn to listen carefully and explain your ideas clearly. Plans only work when people understand them.
